hook: You know Romans 8:28. But did you know the very next verse says what the “good” is?
story:
Before reading this verse, look at the man who wrote it.

In another letter he lists what following Christ had cost him. “Five times I received forty stripes minus one”, he writes. “Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I suffered shipwreck.” A night and a day adrift on the open sea. Hunger. Cold. Danger on every road.

This is not a man who thinks life is gentle. And he is the one who writes, without hesitating, “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God”.

He does not say that all things are good. He carried the scars that say otherwise. He says that God is at work in all of them.
moment:
Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, in the capital of the empire, and he does not pretend their life is easy. A few lines before this verse he speaks of “the sufferings of this present time”. A few lines after it he asks what could ever separate them from the love of Christ, and runs through the list: “oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword”.

Between those two passages stands this sentence. It is written for people who are living inside the list.
around: The promise is given to a particular group: “those who love God”, who are “called according to his purpose”. The next verse names that purpose: “to be conformed to the image of his Son”.
readings:
Some people hear this verse as a promise that everything happens for a reason and will turn out well. Paul says something more careful. He does not call every event good. He says God works in all of them toward one good, and the next verse names it: to make his people like his Son.

Christians have also long discussed the words that follow, about those whom God foreknew and called. Some traditions stress that God chooses and holds his people from first to last. Others stress the free answer of the person who loves God. Both hear the verse as comfort: whatever comes, those who belong to God are not in the hands of chance.
argued:
In 1663 the Puritan preacher Thomas Watson wrote a whole book on this one verse and called it A Divine Cordial, a medicine for the soul. He pushed the promise as far as it will go: even the sins of the godly, once they turn from them, are made to serve their good. [[watson]] Then he added a warning at once: no one should take this teaching as an excuse to sin.

In 1924 President Calvin Coolidge applied the verse to a whole nation. Unveiling a statue of the Methodist bishop Francis Asbury in Washington, he said the founders constantly reminded Americans that all things work together for good to them that love God.

Others today push back on the way the verse is often used. On her podcast Everything Happens, Kate Bowler, a Duke professor who was once told her cancer was incurable, talked it through with the New Testament scholar N. T. Wright. Wright read it as God working all things together with those who love him, and said: [[wright]] Bowler called that a very different reading from the version stitched on pillows.

A Puritan’s medicine, a president’s providence, a scholar’s call to work alongside God: each takes all things seriously, and each means something different by good.
point: The “good” here is becoming like Christ, and Paul says it in a chapter that expects trouble. The verse does not promise that every event is good or that life will become comfortable. It promises that nothing, hardship included, falls outside what God works together for that purpose.
